name: Unfavorable Semicircle
title: Two Videos Every Minute, Then the Channel Vanished
claims: A YouTube account called Unfavorable Semicircle was created in March 2015 | 1
The channel began uploading large numbers of videos on April 5 | 1
Videos were titled with the Sagittarius symbol, a random six-digit number, or both | 1
Most videos lacked a description | 1
Videos often show abstract, pixelated images | 1
Some videos show a single dot in a field of solid brown | 1
Some videos have no sound, others have distorted sound | 1
One completely silent video was 11 hours long | 1
Videos are blurry, dark, with "constellations" of dots in random arrangements | 2
In some videos a heavily muffled male voice recites letters or numbers | 2
Most clips last four or five seconds | 2
Tens of thousands of videos were published | 2
Uploads came at a rate of about two every minute | 2
Two per minute is 120 per hour and nearly 3,000 per day (calculation from the cited rate) | 2
A community formed on Reddit to investigate | 1, 2
One user compiled a database of videos, and a handful offered to transcribe verbal content | 2
Efforts to decode ranged from analysing the dot constellations to questioning the Sagittarius symbol | 2
Lock and Delock were seen by some as keys to the mystery | 1
Lock is over 27 minutes with intense flashing colours and warped audio | 2
A viewer found the videos creepy and felt desensitised after watching many | 2
A viewer said Lock and Delock were the main reason he stayed involved | 2
At 1:26 in Delock a viewer heard what sounded like a man whispering but was unsure; kids singing follows | 2
A user slowed down and sped up Delock's audio and found little | 2
Theories included a test channel, the "work of a disturbed mind", and a numbers station | 2
Numbers stations broadcast seemingly nonsensical, actually coded messages and have been used since World War One | 2
A computer security specialist said a numbers station was probably "too complex" | 1, 2
One Redditor suggested a recruitment tool for Google | 2
The specialist said puzzles are normally announced in some way, albeit subtly | 2
One investigator leaned toward the videos being the output of a bot performing a test | 2
Another thought it could be an "elaborate puzzle" | 2
Webdriver Torso featured random coloured shapes and high-pitched tones and prompted conspiracy theories | 2
Webdriver Torso turned out to be Google's own method of testing content delivery on YouTube | 2
The specialist suspected another test but admitted it was not clear what was going on, and noted much effort went into the videos | 2
Google was not able to provide a comment when asked | 2
The specialist said government agencies are known to plant red herrings that soak up the opposition's time, and the curious can become unintended victims | 2
One follower said he did not feel anything sinister was going on but wanted it solved | 2
Another said "Everyone likes a good mystery" | 2
The BBC article was published 25 February 2016 | 2
A few hours after the article, the channel was suspended without explanation | 1, 2
A user claiming to be the creator said in a Twitter post the goal was to "upload the most number of YouTube videos ever" | 1
The same user said secondarily it was "to see if people would watch something truly and unknowable" | 1
The same user hoped to fill some of the "Internet Mystery" space left by Webdriver Torso | 1
In June 2022 an anonymous X user said the channel was an outsider art project | 1
The BBC called it "YouTube's strangest mystery" | 1
It has been called one of the Top 10 Weirdest YouTube Channels | 1

sources.title: The quest to solve YouTube’s strangest mystery
